utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, can everyone hear me well, the interpreters, everybody? In that case, can we begin, is the Defence ready, General Blaskic, the Prosecution, the assistants? Of course, we are ready too, so it is Mr. Cayley who will continue on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness, Mr. President, is a witness that wishes to be heard in closed session. I have spoken with Mr. Nobilo, he is not in disagreement with this process. It is entirely within your hands. He has already testified in another trial in the Tribunal and there are now reasons which necessitate him wishing to be heard in closed session. I can go into detail in closed session if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the other testimony, did he testify in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He did not, your Honour, no, but there are now reasons why he does wish to testify in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is in agreement. Mr. Registrar, please establish a closed session while Mr. Cayley explains to us the main outlines of the testimony. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The policeman essentially agreed to do that and then transported Witness Z to the Kaonik Prison, where Witness Z remained for a considerable period of time. Witness Z will testify about his experiences in the Kaonik Prison, he will describe the conditions there and he will describe his experiences as a forced labourer at three different locations in and around Vitez and Busovaca. Ultimately, Mr. President, he was exchanged. He will testify that he lost approximately 17 kilograms of weight while he was in captivity. Mr. President, the testimony of Witness Z relates to count 1, persecution, specifically paragraphs 6, 6.2 through 6.6, and paragraph 7. It relates to counts 2 to 4, paragraph 8, unlawful attacks on civilians. It relates to counts 5 through 10, the wilful killing and serious injury, paragraph 9 of the indictment. It relates to counts 11 through 13, plunder of property, paragraph 10. Then it relates to counts 15 through 20 dealing with the inhumane treatment of detainees, hostages and human shields. That concludes my summary, Mr. President and your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional questions? How long did you think that this witness will be here?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please have the witness brought in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you hear me? I will call you Witness Z, as you are under protective measures. We would give you a piece of paper with your first and last name, but please do not say it, simply confirm that it is your identity. Is this your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So from now on, we will call you Witness Z. You have accepted to come to this trial as a witness, asked by the Prosecutor. This is the trial of General Blaskic, who is here. Please would you take the oath, this is a declaration you have to read, please remain seated and read in your language the solemn declaration that is given to you. WITNESS Z (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor gave us the main outline of your testimony and the events of which you seem to have been a witness. Now the Prosecutor will ask you some questions and he will let you speak, it may be he will lead you. There is no need for fear, you are here under the protection of the International Criminal Tribunal and your identity is protected, your voice is protected. Please, you can speak without any fear, the Trial Chamber is listening to you. Mr. Prosecutor? Examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Witness Z.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z, are you a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, did you live in the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you employed as a (redacted) at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, were you a civilian or were you a member of the army or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Territorial Defence as a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, did you return from Split after having driven, been on the road for about 20 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember the approximate date when you returned to Busovaca from that long haul, that long trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 25th, the 24th, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Witness Z, I am going to ask you to relate the story that you have told me to the judges, but I am going to divide it into two parts. I am going to ask you to tell the judges what happened to you after you returned to Busovaca up to the point where you arrived at Kaonik Prison, and then I will ask you some questions. Then I will ask you to relate to the judges the second part of your story, that is what happened to you when you were in Kaonik Prison. If I could have for the first part of the witness's testimony Exhibit 249 shown to the witness and given to counsel and the Trial Chamber? Mr. President, your Honours and counsel, this is an exhibit similar to many we have seen in this trial, it is an enlargement of Exhibit 216, an aerial image and it contains a legend at the back. Witness Z, you have had a chance to examine an aerial image and you have indicated on that image certain locations, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, you will be telling us a narrative form of testimony but so we could illustrate your testimony, can you tell us what number 1 is very briefly, what number 2 is very briefly and what number 3 is on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 is my house. Number 2 is the barn where I spent a night. Number 3 is the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the green line that is on the Exhibit 249 the path that you took from your house and ultimately arrived at the police station at number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please tell the judges what happened to you after you returned to Busovaca in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before the Witness Z continues, I would like to organise our work. Maybe before he starts with his statement, we can have our break, because we have to end today at 5.30 at the very latest. I do not think that we will be able to hear other witnesses today Mr. Harmon, but we will see, so we could start again at 4.30 and then continue for about an hour. In case we will not be able to start with another witness, this witness will have to come back in two weeks or more. We will talk of it later. I think that this is the way we are going to work, so we will resume at 4.30. (4.10 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness Z, could you please tell the judges what happened to you after you returned to Busovaca in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After having spent 20 days in Split, I returned by car to Busovaca, where I was meant to go on to Zenica and unload food. I returned home as I always did. I did not find anyone at home. My wife and a five month old baby had left in the meantime. I stayed there, I spent the night in my house that night and the next day I went out to see whether any of the neighbours were there, and I found Nezrudin, Nusret Begovic, I had a talk with him and he told me that in the town of Busovaca, a number of Muslim businesses had been blown up, cafes, shops and the rest. I asked who else was around and so I went out and in an about an hour or less, a policeman came, by name Ivica Vidovic, and he told me not to leave my house and if there were any more of us to gather there, that there would be no problems, just for us to stay home. Husanovic Fikret was also there, Midhat Hadzibegovic, Nijaz Neslanovic and I told them to come to my place, so that we should stay there, and we spent the whole day there, sitting around and late in the afternoon, we saw a soldier about 200 metres from my house talking to Luka Lovric, who was pointing at our house. The soldier came to the door. Actually, before he entered, Fikret Husanovic said that there should not be any problems because he was his neighbour, his neighbour Josip. The soldier came in, he had a pistol in his hand, and probably because of the surprise, the pistol went off and he fired into the floor. He was scared himself and he went off immediately, having said that there would be no problems. Five or ten minutes later, he came back with two more men. He entered, he made us sit down and he started questioning us. While he was questioning us, another one with a camouflage hat was opening the cupboards. He started asking Midhat what his name was, where he came from, and then Nijaz. When he reached Fikret he said to him, "there is no need to ask you because I know you". He asked us whether anyone had searched us for weapons. We said that Ivica Vidovic had. He said that he was a commie and what had he to do with it. We stayed there, then he asked Fikret whether he knew somebody by the name of Oliver. Fikret said he did, then he told him that Oliver had been killed. He asked, "do you know, Fikret, who killed him?". Fikret said, "I do not". He said, "the Turks", repeating three or four times, "the Turks killed him". Then he asked the other two, "what are we going to do with the balijas, the Turks?". He nodded with his head, telling them to go outside into the hallway. They went out and in about a minute or two weapons could be heard. They entered the house and opened fire on us. Three of us got killed. I lay there among them and when they had emptied their weapons, I heard boots walking out of the house, and through the window or rather the door of the balcony, I saw a light and a strong explosion, and I do not remember anything after that, what exactly happened. They had insignia of the HVO police here with the word "Vitez", this was the insignia worn by Ivica, I did not notice what the other two were wearing. They were armed with rifles. Afterwards, when I came to, I crawled out because the others were dead and I went to the barn of Salih Hodzic. I stayed there until the morning. In the morning around 7.00, I headed towards the police station, and I got close to the police when I observed Slavko Katava, a policeman whom I called and asked him whether I may approach. He said I could if I was not armed, so I walked up and he asked me what was wrong. I asked him to take me where there were other Muslims, and so he took me to Kaonik where almost all detainees were Muslims and so I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z, let me interrupt you there just to clarify a couple of points about your testimony, the first part of your testimony. Did these events, the murder of your friends, occur on 26th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your three friends who were murdered, were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the men who came into the house and committed the murders was wearing an HVO military police badge that had "Vitez" on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the others also identify themselves as being part of the military police from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were the other people who were with the man with the badge from the military police in Vitez, were they wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to murdering your friends, did they take any personal property from you or your friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said -- he said that if we had any gold or money to put it on the table. We did not have anything, at least that is what we said, except for Midhat Hadzibegovic, who took off his watch, but it had an inscription because his father had received it after 50 years of service, so he gave it back to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z, you eventually made your way to the centre of Busovaca where you said you talked to a policeman by the name of Katava and he eventually took you to the HVO military prison in Kaonik. Did you inform the policeman about the murders that had taken place the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges why you did not tell him about the murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not dare, I did not trust anyone any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now let me pick up your testimony about Kaonik Prison and before we get to that, I would like to have Exhibit 250 handed to you and to the judges. This will relate to the next part of your testimony. Witness Z, you are going to be in the next part of your testimony referring to three locations where the HVO forced you to commit -- to dig trenches and you have indicated to me and I have then prepared this exhibit, the locations where you were forced to dig trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those areas indicated are Strane, Milavice and on the far left of Exhibit 250 there is a green over the word Kovacevac. You will be referring to that area as Bare in your testimony, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you testify digging at a location known as Bare, that is the location we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Witness Z, carry on with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So once I arrived in Kaonik, the camp, I found many Muslims there before me and I was immediately put in a cell in which there was between 15 and 20 of us and that same day, we were called to dig trenches. They came by car to pick us up and they took us to Milavice. We spent the day and the night digging, so half a day and one night. They did not give us anything to eat, we had to work hard and then the next day, a replacement came, another group came and we were taken back to Kaonik. After a rest of, I do not know, maybe one day, I went to Kovacevac, to Bare. I was digging there from the morning until the evening. They brought us back, I spent the night, and then again I was taken to Milavice for digging one day, one night and another day. Digging there in addition to me was Nedzad Nusretbegovic, Faruk Tulic and some others whose names I cannot recall, some 20 of us. There was Juzbasic Saban. We were digging trenches. Saban was about 10 metres behind us digging a trench 2 metres by 1.5 metres. Three HVO soldiers came with masks on their faces, and they said that the balija had to be shot and all of us had to be killed, and they forced us into this hole that Saban had dug. They ordered us to look down and to fall on our knees. They cocked their rifles and there was silence, and then Faruk Tulic was taken out for disobedience, for not bending his head low enough, and then they kicked him for a while and threw him back amongst us afterwards. I later returned and when we set off near the cafe called, "Jedane Splave", or "The Eleven Blue Ones", a group was waiting for us and Nedzad Nusretbegovic was beaten there in the head, he was kicked in the head and he had concussion from this. Then after all this, we got back to Kaonik. Later, after a short rest, they took us to Strane to dig trenches. I was digging there for about an hour and with me was a boy of five from Jajce, his surname was Begic, and he was wounded in the cheek with a sniper and I was hit in the armpit. Drago, who was guarding us at the time, the owner of the "Sunce" or "Sun Cafe", took us for treatment. He treated us and took us to the infirmary, to the medical centre. Afterwards we were taken back to Kaonik and I do not know how but the manager called me to talk to me, asked me whether I was afraid, whether I was in pain and he said that I would not be taken to dig trenches or to do any forced labour until my exchange, so that I was put in a cell where there were already men who were being spared forced labour. That would roughly be what happened until my exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date of your exchange, Witness Z, or how many days you spent in captivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not exactly remember the date, but I spent 12 days in detention and I was exchanged by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose weight as a result of your captivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lost some 17 kilos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions to clarify your testimony about your stay in the Kaonik camp. First of all, you said when you arrived you were placed in a cell with about 15 to 20 other people; were those all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the dimensions of the cell in which you and the 15 to 20 other Muslims were being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2.5 metres by 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first night you were taken out to dig trenches, and you were taken to a location in, was it Milavice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the location in Milavice where you were forced to dig trenches, were you relieving another group of people who had been digging trenches, and if so how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We relieved another group, there were some 20, 25 people in our group and also when we finished digging, another group relieved us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were digging trenches in your group, were they all Muslims and were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that the group you had relieved and later the group that relieved your group were also civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next location where you went to dig trenches was at the location on the map you have referred to as Bare. How many civilians were taken with you to Bare to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those 15 to 20 people all Muslims and all civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Bare, were you also relieved by another group of forced labourers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also some 20 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they appear to be civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you eventually were taken to Milavice for a second time, how many Muslims were taken to Milavice with you to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 20, 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Milavice, were you forced to shout anything to a front-line position that was nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what you were forced to shout?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Where are you balijas?", we had to swear at their mother and then, "come on balijas, what are you waiting for, we are ready, we are waiting for you", something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court very very briefly what also happened to Saban while he was at the front-lines at Milavice. I am referring to the incident where they covered him with dirt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that thing where it seemed that they would kill us, shoot us, Saban stayed on. Then they took him and covered him, put him in earth as if they were to bury him alive and once they covered him with earth, not completely, but they started to cover him with earth, they took him out. He was kicked as well and then they had to -- they said they had to wash him and then they brought water and washing him, they sprayed him with water so as to supposedly give him a bath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the temperature outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was January, minus 15 degrees, so minus 15 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were guarding you at Milavice and Bare and at Strane HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to now turn your attention to the location of Strane. The translation, at least the English translation, Witness Z, that I received was that a 5 year old boy was wounded. Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not 5, 15 year old boy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At that location, Witness Z, the 15 year old boy was shot; where was he shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cheek, beneath his eye, a bullet passed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the armpit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later in your testimony, you said that you went back to the Kaonik military and you met with the manager of the prison. Who was the manager of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Zlatko Aleksovski later on. I was brought to him and all the sparing was given by Ivo Milic, who was a guard. When he took him to his room, he said, amongst others, you are not going to work and there was a very large book there, some kind of a diary. At the back of it, the cover, he said that I had to be spared from labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he kept some kind of a book, a record of people who were engaged in labour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to one other aspect and that is while you were in custody, were you informed or told by some of your fellow detainees about human shields being used at Merdani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify the people who told you about being used as human shields and tell the judges what they told you had occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when they put me in the room where there were people spared from forced labour, in there was Sead Delkic and his brother Besim Delkic, Semin was there also, Arnaud, whose first name I cannot recall, and he said that while we were digging somewhere, that they went to Merdani as human shields and they did not know, there were 15 of them who had been called out, they gave him a rope, then they tied them in three groups of five and then put them so tied up on to buses and they drove them from Kaonik by the old railroad towards the village of Merdani. There they put them in three rows and by loudspeaker, they were calling for surrender and then they started going on. According to their story, from Merdani there was fire that came, the shooting started so they retreated. They were escorted by some kind of an armed vehicle made of steel which had semi-automatic rifle on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Z, who did they say made them into forced shields and put them into that dangerous situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers. I do not know. They did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention very briefly to a statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 23rd February 1995. You pointed out to me a number of serious mistakes in this statement last night, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You informed me, after having this statement read to you, that the reference on page 4 that says that you were a human shield at Merdani is incorrect, and what you had told the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor was that you had heard the story about human shields but that you personally were not a human shield, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also pointed out to me another mistake in this statement, and that is that on the first page in the first full paragraph that refers to the shooting and the murder of your three friends in Busovaca, it says that you were grazed on the side and fell down and in fact that is incorrect, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were grazed -- you actually received some kind of a shock on your head as a result of an explosion while you were at the location of the house where your friends were murdered, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I have concluded my examination of Witness Z. I would ask to introduce into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibits 249 and 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I enquire if either of those are to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. If we could have Exhibit 249 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we have heard Witness Z very difficult testimony, what you went through, and now we will start cross-examination as I realised. Mr. Hayman has started almost in your stead. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are co-counsel, so it is not as important who does what. Witness Z, you said that you were a civilian. Is it correct that you belong to the third platoon, the third company of the Busovaca unit that was under command of Vahid Hajdarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a company of the Territorial Defence before 33rd Mountaineering Brigade was formed. Could the usher please show the list of the third company and under number 87, would you look it up and please confirm or deny that this is your name and are these the names of the members of your company. Unfortunately we have only one copy of it, but we will ask for it to be copied because we never know what we need really during cross-examination. Please look up this list, are these the members of your company and on page 2, please look up at number 87. We cannot put it on the ELMO because we could not -- would otherwise disclose the identity of the witness. So this is the list of the members of your company and your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you a civilian when you came to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that when you arrived at Kaonik you came to the 33rd Brigade that had his headquarters at Kacuni; does it belong to the 6th Mountain Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 7th Mountain Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to which corps it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the III Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to object. I did not go into details about military structure with this witness. This is beyond the scope of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your objective, Mr. Nobilo, could you explain that to me? Yes, he said that he was a civilian, you are trying to put him -- to contradict him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have just ended with that part of my cross-examination. The reason why I asked that was because the witness said that he had been a civilian and as such he was at Kaonik and there were only civilians at Kaonik; I was only trying to prove that he was not a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness also testified he was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, that means that we are now in direct examination. Mr. Nobilo, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In any case, I have ended with this part of my examination. You come back from your trip and your family is not there. Did you manage to contact your family later on, did you contact your wife by phone, did you have an explanation why they were not at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went to my parents, I had a baby that was two months old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the neighbouring municipality where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which municipality was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those friends of yours who were with you in the house, had their families also gone away? Did they leave their families in their houses and they were with you in that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them left and some of them were there. The children were mostly out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside, I do not know where they went, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask your friend why did all these families leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because two days before I arrived a young man was killed in the house by the name of Mirsad Delija, so people decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they expect a conflict between the army of BH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not expect it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ivica Vidovic tell you to all go into the house and get together for your own security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he came into the house when there was an attempted burglary and murder and that there was a neighbour by the name of Josip there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that Josip Relata?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you addressed the civilian policeman and you did not tell him what had happened, did you ask from him to put you to Kaonik, to go where the Muslims were for your own safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the military police of the HVO beat up certain HVO members who had stolen things and murdered a person by the name of Ermin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the last day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the HVO police had beaten up an HVO soldier because he was violent against a Muslim, because Ermin was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about human shields. Who exactly told you about human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delkic Besim and Delkic Sead, Arnovic Ermin and somebody by the surname of Arnaud whose surname I cannot recall and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of them telling the story or just one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them, there was a group of them because they were all with me in the same cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these people from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone killed then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were either you -- did either you or them report to Aleksovski or anyone else from the prison administration what happened at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I do not know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have ended my cross-examination. Excuse me, please, this document, the list of the members of the unit, we would like to be admitted into evidence as sealed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no objection and we would ask that a copy of that be furnished to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I am looking at my colleagues, Judge Riad, do you have any questions, Judge Shahabuddeen? No questions. Witness Z, you have been very brave, you have been through horrible things during that war, the Trial Chamber has heard you, now you can go back to your home and hopefully regain some peace. Please now remain seated while the Trial Chamber goes out. This is our last hearing this session, and now we will distribute to the parties a schedule done by the Registry. You will have all the calculations in there with the explanations. You will realise that we are not in advance. When we have nine or ten calendar days, in fact there are five days -- we have got five days of hearings. There were some incidents, and please try and reconsider and reflect upon all these data, and also see whether during cross-examination maybe you could find some more operational methods. Having said that, for the time being we will stick to the decision, the ruling from 17th December by which the Defence has got a number of days allocated to it; also you, Mr. Prosecutor, have got 34 days left to end the Prosecution case. In case you have no other remarks now, we will adjourn. Tomorrow we have no hearings because of the technical and the plenary sessions. Any comments? The hearing is adjourned. (5.25 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Wednesday, 18th February 1998) 23 24 25
